clips.stepText: When prices slump, managers ask two distinct questions. Breaking even means price covers total unit cost. Shutting down immediately only makes sense if price falls below average variable cost. Suppose a tailor pays five thousand naira rent and spends three thousand on cloth. Earning four thousand still shrinks her loss.

clips.stepText: Why hold cash in your pocket instead of spending it right away? Economist John Maynard Keynes spotted three reasons. First, you buy daily bread and bus rides. Second, you save for sudden hospital bills or a flat tyre. Third, you wait to buy cheap shares or lend at higher rates. Your cash plus bank deposits form total money supply.

clips.stepText: How quickly does cash jump from hand to hand? Suppose one two-naira note pays a tailor, a butcher, an electrician, and a hotelier in one day. That single note settled eight naira of business, giving a speed of four. When extra money chases unchanged goods, prices rise proportionally. Higher prices mean each naira buys fewer items.

clips.stepText: When prices keep climbing month after month, inflation eats your wallet. Imagine a tin of milk jumping from one hundred naira to one hundred and twenty naira. Too much buyer spending causes demand-pull inflation, while costlier fuel or wages trigger cost-push inflation. Borrowers gain because they repay with weaker cash. Falling prices, called deflation, hurt jobs instead.

clips.stepText: Unlike high-street banks, the Central Bank of Nigeria never serves ordinary walk-in customers. It prints naira, holds federal funds, and rescues troubled banks as lender of last resort. Suppose inflation heats up. It sells government securities to commercial banks to drain their lending cash. Raising the discount rate and cash ratio also slows credit alongside tighter government budgets.

clips.stepText: How does one bank deposit multiply across the economy? Imagine you deposit ten thousand naira when the reserve rule is ten percent. Your bank keeps one thousand and lends nine thousand. That loan gets deposited elsewhere, creating another loan round. Deposits grow until total money hits one hundred thousand, though cash hoarding or scarce collateral limits it.

clips.stepText: Watch out for two related traps on inflation questions. First, higher prices never raise money's value. When food gets costlier, your naira buys less, so its value actually drops. Second, price controls rarely cure demand-pull inflation. Without extra production, buyers still chase scarce goods, creating long queues, hoarding, and thriving black markets.

Also read carefully for total deposits versus net new credit.

National product tracks what Nigerian citizens earn worldwide. Suppose a Nigerian engineer earns wages in London. That counts toward our national product, not domestic product. Subtract machine wear, remove indirect taxes, and add subsidies to find factor income.

That food raises her family's welfare yet never passes through a market stall or tax ledger. Unpaid housework, smuggling, and missing shop records hide real output. High national totals also ignore pollution and unequal wealth.

Putting five hundred, one hundred and fifty, two hundred, and thirty together yields eight hundred and eighty billion naira.

clips.stepText: Next, shift from domestic borders to citizen ownership. Net foreign factor income is negative thirty billion here. That means foreign earners sent home more than citizens remitted back. Adding negative thirty brings gross national product to eight hundred and fifty billion. Subtracting fifty billion for worn machinery leaves eight hundred billion.

clips.stepText: One final adjustment gives true factor earnings. Shop prices carry indirect sales taxes that go to government, not workers or factory owners. Meanwhile, government subsidies kept shop prices artificially lower than actual production costs. So subtract sixty billion in indirect taxes and add twenty billion in subsidies. That brings national income at factor cost to seven hundred and sixty billion.

clips.stepText: Two items secretly inflate national income answers in exams. Never add raw materials alongside finished goods made from them. Doing so counts the exact same output twice. Also throw out transfer payments like pensions, gifts, or unemployment benefits. Recipients get cash without producing any new goods or services.

clips.stepText: Do not mix up borders with passports. A foreign factory inside Lagos adds to Nigeria's domestic product. Meanwhile, a Nigerian doctor in London adds to our national product. Also guard the multiplier denominator carefully. Always invert the saving fraction, never the consuming fraction itself.

clips.stepText: A high average income per person can easily fool you. Averages hide whether wealth sits with a tiny elite while millions struggle. Official figures also miss home-grown farm food and unpaid family care. Furthermore, extra working hours reduce leisure. Heavy factory pollution can even lift output while harming daily life.

clips.stepText: Remember these four pillars for national income questions. Count output, income, or spending once by dropping intermediate inputs and transfer payments. Step cleanly from domestic output to national product and net factor cost. Finally, invert the saving propensity. That tells you how strongly new spending multiplies through the circular flow.
